transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-16
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Ava Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Reddy (BlueMesa CTO), Marcus Li (BlueMesa ML Eng), Hannah Cole (BlueMesa Product)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
- Focus: pilot unit economics, tokens per dollar, caching and batching tradeoffs, next steps for benchmark tests.
- Key result: prefix/KV caching shows biggest cost reduction for BlueMesa prompt mix (~2.6-3x lower tokens/$ on common flows).
- Open: quantization impact on quality vs cost, dedicated vs hosted for 99th percentile latency.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Samir here from Redwood — I'm the AE on this pilot. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Priya: Priya Reddy, CTO, BlueMesa. Marcus and Hannah are here too.
[00:12] Marcus: Marcus Li, ML Eng. Hey.
[00:14] Hannah: Hannah Cole, product. Hi all.
[00:16] Ava: Ava Chen, Redwood SE. I'll lead the perf bits today if that's ok.
[00:20] Samir: Yup perfect. Agenda — quick recap of last week's numbers, walk through updated pilot_benchmarks.csv, deep-dive on caching and batching tradeoffs, then align on next steps.

[00:36] Ava: Alright, I'll share screen — (link to pilot_benchmarks.csv) — note: there's a new sheet called tokens-per-dollar that uses your representative prompt distribution we got last week. Caveat: transcription may garble some metric names, but numbers are solid.
[00:50] Marcus: Quick Q — that prompt distribution includes the Q&A flow and the long context summarization?
[00:55] Ava: Yes, we split into short Q (median 120 tokens), medium (600 tokens), and long summarize (avg 3k tokens) — we used the sampling you sent, plus some synthetic edge-cases to ensure tail.

[01:10] Priya: What's the headline? You mentioned caching gave 2–3x improvement last time. Are we seeing the same?
[01:15] Ava: Short answer: yes but with nuance. For your most common short-Q flows, prefix/KV caching reduces per-response compute by about 2.6x on average — because many calls reuse the same context prefixes. For long summarize flows, caching less useful. We also modeled batching: if you allow 50–100ms extra latency, batching can give an additional 10–25% token/sec/$ improvement for medium requests, but for short Qs at strict p50 < 100ms SLOs the batching window almost never fills.
[01:46] Marcus: Are these numbers with quantized model or FP16?
[01:49] Ava: These are mixed — baseline is FP16/AMP on the hosted endpoint. We also included a column for q4_0 quantization, which reduces token compute by ~1.8x but we saw a small BLEU-like delta in one of your summarization prompts — not huge but measurable. We captured a simple QA-quality metric in the CSV.

[02:10] Hannah: Can you remind us how tokens/sec/$ is computed? I want to make sure our finance folks get the same thing.
[02:15] Ava: Sure — we take total model tokens produced + input tokens, map the GPU-second cost using our observed GPU utilization per request, then normalize to $ using a blended infra cost (hosted list price minus pilot discount). It's in the sheet called methodology. There are a few assumptions — steady-state vs burst, KV cache hit rate assumptions (we ran low/med/high scenarios).

[02:38] Priya: Burstiness is our worry — peak QPS can jump 6x for short windows. Will caching still help during burst?
[02:45] Ava: Caching helps reduce compute per request, so it reduces overall capacity need, which helps during bursts. But if your burst is new unique prefixes, cache hit rate drops and benefit reduces. Also for burst smoothing, Dedicated with reserved capacity or Redwood's burst policy can help — you can reserve base and enable burst lanes.

[03:05] Marcus: On the dedicated vs hosted question — our SLA target is p95 < 180ms and p99 < 500ms for short Qs, is that realistic on hosted?
[03:12] Samir: Hosted can meet p95 in many regions, but p99 depends on noise, multitenancy, and model size. For guaranteed p99 you often choose Dedicated or Private where isolation gives more consistent tail latency. We can show empirical traces from similar pilots in the CSV.

[03:32] Ava: Also, note the KV cache hit rate we used for BlueMesa short flows was 48% — that's moderate. If Marcus can change prompt surface to include more stable prefixes, we can push hit rate to 70–80% and the economics get much better.

[03:48] Marcus: Right — I think we can template the prompts more. I'll add an engineering ticket for that.

[03:55] Hannah: On quantization, what's the plan to validate quality? If q4 gives 1.8x cost reduction but degrades summaries slightly, how do we test?
[04:02] Ava: We recommend staged validation: run a small A/B on a held-out prompt set (we can host the eval harness), monitor your specific quality metrics (ROUGE/QA F1 or human annotated accept rate). We'll help set up the A/B and run statistical significance checks.

[04:20] Priya: Any thoughts on caching store? We prefer not to hold customer PII in shared caches.
[04:26] Samir: Understood — Redwood's hosted cache can be configured with TTLs and scrubbers; for sensitive data we recommend using Private or Dedicated and an encrypt-at-rest KMS — or apply a redact step before caching. We can detail options in the security doc.

[04:44] Marcus: Can you run a KV test where we pin a 4k context to simulate large conversation summaries and see cache eviction behavior?
[04:49] Ava: Yes — we'll schedule that. We'll also record cache hit/miss traces and token savings per request.

[04:56] Samir: On the cost model — there's a model-level lever (smaller model family + higher prompting) versus system-level (batching + caching + quant). For BlueMesa's mix, caching+quant seems the biggest win. Batching helps if you accept slight latency increases.

[05:15] Hannah: From product standpoint we have to decide acceptable latency for different flows — short Qs need high responsiveness; summary jobs can tolerate 2–3s. So tiering makes sense.

[05:27] Priya: If we do tiering, what's easiest? Dedicated for short Qs and hosted for long jobs?
[05:31] Samir: Exactly — or a single route with smart routing: low-latency pool for the short Q route and cheaper batch pool for long summaries. Redwood's routing can do that per API key or route.

[05:44] Marcus: Any ballpark numbers for tokens/sec/$ after we push hit rate to 70% and enable q4?
[05:49] Ava: Looking at the sheet, short Q tokens/$ improved roughly 4.8x vs baseline when combining 70% cache hit + q4 quantization. Medium requests see ~2.5–3x. Long summaries see smaller gains because most token spend is on the generation not repeated prefixes.

[06:10] Priya: That's promising. Next, what do you need from us this week?
[06:13] Samir: Marcus — representative prompts + QPS target. Hannah — confirm success metric (max $/response and acceptable p99). We'll push the KV test and share updated CSV by Thursday.

[06:24] Marcus: I'll upload prompts to s3 today.
[06:26] Hannah: I'll sync with finance and send target metrics by Friday.
[06:29] Priya: Also send the security appendix for caching and private deploy options.
[06:33] Samir: Yes — I'll attach the security.pdf and the pilot_benchmarks.csv after the call.

[06:38] (brief cross talk)
[06:40] Ava: One more technical note — when batching we observed an increase in GPU memory pressure which can slightly increase evictions on very large contexts; it's a tradeoff with throughput. We'll include memory/latency contour plots in the CSV.
[06:55] Marcus: Good to know. We'll try the prompt template changes first then run your KV test.

[07:02] Samir: Great. Recap/next steps: Samir shares benchmark CSV + security appendix by 2025-09-18; Marcus uploads prompts by 2025-09-19; Ava runs KV/prefix cache test and shares logs by 2025-09-22; schedule quantization deep-dive week of 2025-09-22.
[07:22] Priya: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[07:24] Hannah: Thanks.
[07:25] Samir: Thanks all, we'll follow up in email with links.

End of transcript.

References and links mentioned during call (not embedded): pilot_benchmarks.csv (shared), security.pdf (Redwood caching and private options), s3://blue-mesa/pilot-prompts (customer upload location).
